newsitem.title: FRANCE: Rich nations pledge $450 mln aid to Cambodia.
newsitem.headline: Rich nations pledge $450 mln aid to Cambodia.

text.p: Donor nations and institutions pledged on Wednesday $450 million in official aid to Cambodia for 1997/98 and urged Phnom Penh to pursue vital economic reforms as it heads for national elections next year.

Rich nations and international organisations, at the end of a two-day meeting at the World Bank here, called on the government to tackle issues which had seen little progress since a meeting of a consultative group last year in Tokyo.

"Donors endorsed the government's reconstruction and development objectives. In support of that programme, a total of $450 million was pledged by donors for 1997/98," the World Bank said in a statement.

But the Cambodian authorities needed to adopt more effective collection and accounting for taxes, ensure the fiscal system was clear and fair, and gather more revenue from logging activities, World Bank official Javad Shirazi told reporters.

"Cambodia is entering a critical phase in the run-up to elections," he said. "The government needs to focus on economic reforms" and ensure "political issues do not destabilise the gains that have been made," he added.
"Revenues need to be collected. They have to go into the public treasury and be properly accounted for so the citizenry and the world know what was collected and where it went," he said.
The United Nations warned in a statement released in Phnom Penh on Wednesday that the government was spending too much money on security forces and failing to meet tax revenue collection targets.
International aid makes up nearly half the annual national budget and about half of yearly government spending goes on defence and security.
Although there were no detailed discussions on any conditions tied to the aid, the message was made very clear that changes needed to be made by the government, Shirazi said.
"Economic developement and management never occur in a vacuum," he said. "There is a need for strong political leadership to ensure economic reforms are not derailed".

Cambodian minister for economy and finance Keat Chhon said although the amount pledged fell short of the $490 million the country needs annually for its three-year plan to 1999, $40 million expected from non-governmental organisations and aid from a "friendly nation" would make up the rest.
"It is up to the Cambodian people to show that the country deserves all that...and earn the credibility of the taxpayers of these countries," he said.
Cambodia received official aid pledges of $500 million for 1996/97, an aid official said.

Chhon said the government had recently adopted laws to improve the tax collection system and aimed to enlarge the tax base so as to increase the gross domestic product by one percent a year. "This is a major challenge," he said.
